title: 🐛 Mission 4: Break R on purpose
text:
⏱️ About 10 minutes · do this in RStudio, using your Mission 1 project
Congratulations. Your job for the next ten minutes is to make R angry, on purpose, in a setting where it doesn’t cost you anything. The point isn’t to learn to avoid errors — you can’t, everyone gets them, every day, forever. The point is to see a handful of them once, calmly, before day one, so they’re familiar instead of frightening.
Open the project from Mission 1 and use R/analysis.R for all of this.

title: 🐛 Mission 4: Break R on purpose
text:
Round 1: break your own path
You already know this one works:
read.csv("data/participants.csv")
Run it, confirm it works. Now:

In your file explorer (not RStudio), rename the data folder to data-old.
Run the exact same line again.
Read the error. It should say something like cannot open file 'data/participants.csv': No such file or directory.
Rename the folder back to data, run it once more, confirm it works again.

This is the Mission 2 mental model made real: R went looking for 🏠 → data → participants.csv, and for a minute, that middle step didn’t exist.






NoteWhy rename to data-old, and not just Data?





On Windows and (usually) macOS, file and folder names are treated as case-insensitive — data and Data point to the same folder, so that swap wouldn’t actually break anything for most of you, and the exercise would quietly fail to make its point. It still matters to match case anyway: the moment a script gets shared with someone on Linux, or run on a university computing cluster, case starts counting for real. Better to build the habit now than get caught out later.

title: 🐛 Mission 4: Break R on purpose
section: Round 2: a small gallery of classics
text:
Round 2: a small gallery of classics
Run each of these, one at a time, and actually read what R says before moving to the next.
mean(age
You’ll notice the Console prompt changes from > to + and nothing happens — R thinks you’re still mid-sentence. Press Esc to cancel it, then look closely: the closing ) is missing.
Mean(age)
Error in Mean(age) : could not find function "Mean"
R is case-sensitive. Mean and mean are two completely different names as far as R is concerned — and only one of them exists.
my data <- 10
Error: unexpected symbol in "my data"
Object names can’t contain spaces. R reads my and data as two separate things and has no idea what to do with them side by side.






TipAnatomy of an error message





Take Error in Mean(age) : could not find function "Mean" apart:

Error in Mean(age) — where it happened: while trying to run Mean(age).
could not find function "Mean" — what went wrong, in R’s own words.

Error messages are R telling you exactly what it was trying to do when it got stuck. They’re not a verdict on you — they’re a debugging hint, written by the machine, for you.

title: 🐛 Mission 4: Break R on purpose
text:
The reframe






Important



Errors are part of programming. The important question is not “Did I get an error?” but “What is R trying to tell me?”


Every single person in this course will see red error text on day one — including the people who’ve used R for years. What changes with experience isn’t how often you see errors, it’s how calmly you read them.
Stuck on one that doesn’t look like these? Check Help! 😱 — same page you’ll reach for during the course itself.
Next up: Mission 5 — Your first research dataset →

text: ⏱️ About 10–15 minutes · do this in RStudio
crumbs: 🗺️ Mission 2: Help R find your files

title: 🗺️ Mission 2: Help R find your files
text:
R needs a starting point
You’ll usually see paths explained like this:

A relative path is relative to your working directory.

Which is correct, and not very useful the first time you read it. Try this instead:






NoteThe mental model



Your RStudio Project (from Mission 1) says:
🏠 “Start looking from here.”
So when your code says:
read_csv("data/study.csv")
it means:
Start at 🏠 → open data → find study.csv.


That’s it. Every relative path (a path that doesn’t start with a drive letter or /) is read as directions from that one starting point — not from your Desktop, not from wherever the file explorer happens to be pointing.
crumbs: 🗺️ Mission 2: Help R find your files

title: 🗺️ Mission 2: Help R find your files
section: Asking R where it thinks it is
text:
Asking R where it thinks it is
Now that you have the mental model, meet the function:
getwd()
Think of it as: “R, where do you think you are right now?” It answers with the folder your Project called 🏠. If you ever get “file not found” and you’re not sure why, getwd() is the first thing to run — it tells you where R is actually starting its search from.
crumbs: 🗺️ Mission 2: Help R find your files

title: 🗺️ Mission 2: Help R find your files
section: Quiz: which path should R use?
text:
Quiz: which path should R use?
Imagine this project:
basic-r/
├── basic-r.Rproj
├── data/
│   └── penguins.csv
└── analysis.R
You’ve opened basic-r.Rproj, and you’re writing code in analysis.R to read penguins.csv. Which path should you use? Click one:

Which path should R use?
A. "penguins.csv"
B. "data/penguins.csv"
C. "basic-r/data/penguins.csv"
D. "C:/Users/Anna/Desktop/basic-r/data/penguins.csv"

title: 🗺️ Mission 2: Help R find your files
text:
Try it yourself
In the project you made in Mission 1:

Open R/analysis.R.
Run getwd() — confirm it points to your my-first-r-project folder.
Add this line and run it:

list.files("data")
You should see participants.csv in the output. If you get character(0) (an empty result) instead, getwd() isn’t pointing where you think — that’s your clue to go back and check you opened the .Rproj file, not a loose script.






WarningA Windows-specific gotcha



Windows shows file paths with backslashes, like data\study.csv. In R, always use forward slashes instead — data/study.csv — even on Windows. A backslash means something special to R, so paths copy-pasted straight from Windows Explorer will usually break.

title: 🚦 Mission 0: Are you R Ready?
text:
⏱️ About 2 minutes · no coding yet

This isn’t a test — there’s no score to fail. It’s just a quick way to see which of the next missions matter most for you. If you’ve never touched R before, expect to answer “not really” a lot, and that’s exactly the point of this whole pre-course.
Read each statement. Be honest, not aspirational.

1. I have R and RStudio installed, and RStudio opens without an error. (Not R alone — you need both. R is the engine, RStudio is the dashboard.)
2. I know what an “RStudio Project” is, and I’ve created one before.
3. If someone asked “what’s your current working directory?”, I could answer without googling it.
4. I know roughly what <-, (), and $ each do in R.
5. When R shows me a red error message, my first reaction is to read it, not to panic.

title: R Ready — Basic R pre-course site
text:
A Quarto website, built as pre-course material for the Basic R course - Aarhus University.
Live at: https://tahereh-gh.github.io/basic-r-course/ Repo: https://github.com/Tahereh-Gh/basic-r-course


Requires Quarto — already installed on this machine.
From the Basic R Course folder (one level up from here), run:
quarto preview r-ready
or, from inside this r-ready folder itself:
quarto preview
Either way: it builds the site, opens it in your default browser automatically, and live-reloads every time you save a .qmd file. Press Ctrl+C in the terminal to stop it.



Content complete: home page, all 7 missions (00–06), and the full Help section. Mission 3 has live, runnable R in the browser (webR); Mission 2 has an interactive click-and-get-feedback quiz; the final challenge ends with an animated “R Passport.”
Published: pushed to GitHub (main branch) and live on GitHub Pages (gh-pages branch). See “Publish to GitHub Pages” below for how to push updates.




Dataset: Missions 1, 5, and 6 all use one small synthetic file, downloads/participants.csv (id/age/group/score, made up, not real course data) — deliberately generic since it wasn’t clear yet whether the course itself would use climate.xlsx or something else. It’s registered in _quarto.yml under project: resources: — if you add more downloadable files, add their folder there too, or Quarto won’t copy them into _site/. If the course settles on a real dataset, swap this file and update the three missions that reference it (search for participants.csv).
Live R (webR): Mission 3 uses the quarto-webr extension (installed under _extensions/coatless/webr/) for in-browser, no-install-needed R cells (```{webr-r}). It needs engine: knitr + filters: [webr] in that page’s front matter — building it requires R + knitr installed locally (they are, on this machine), but viewing the page needs nothing but a browser, since webR itself runs client-side via WebAssembly. First cell on a page takes a few seconds to initialize (downloads the R runtime); later cells on the same page are instant and share the same R session/objects.
Interactive quiz: the click-and-get-feedback widget (Mission 2) and the R Passport (final challenge) are both plain HTML/CSS/JS — no extra dependency. Markup pattern and behavior live in _includes/site-scripts.html (shared JS, injected on every page via include-after-body in _quarto.yml) and the .rr-quiz / .rr-passport rules in styles.scss. To add another quiz elsewhere, copy the .rr-quiz block from missions/02-paths.qmd and change data-answer/data-option/data-feedback.
RStudio diagram (Mission 1): a real screenshot (images/rstudio-panes.png) with the ①②③④ pane labels and highlight boxes overlaid via CSS (.rr-pane-box / .rr-pane-badge in styles.scss), not baked into the image itself — see the .rr-diagram-photo block in missions/01-projects.qmd. To swap in a newer screenshot later, replace the PNG and nudge the left/top/width/height percentages on the overlay <span>s if the pane layout has shifted.
Missions 4 and 6 deliberately avoid case-only filename changes (e.g. data → Data) as a way to trigger an error — Windows and default Mac filesystems are case-insensitive, so that wouldn’t actually break for most students. They use real renames/wrong filenames instead, which fail everywhere.
The Help → “Tahereh or Genona” names are hardcoded in help/index.qmd; update if that page ever gets used for a different course or instructor pairing.




To update the live site after editing content:

Commit your changes on main as usual (git add, git commit, git push).
From inside r-ready/, run:

bash republish.sh
republish.sh re-renders the site and pushes the result to gh-pages (the worktree dance below, scripted). Or do it by hand:
git worktree add --detach /c/ghpwt-tmp
cd /c/ghpwt-tmp
git checkout --orphan gh-pages
git rm -rf . -q
cp -r "/path/to/r-ready/_site/." .
touch .nojekyll
git add -A && git commit -m "Publish site"
git push origin gh-pages -f
cd - && git worktree remove /c/ghpwt-tmp --force
Why not quarto publish gh-pages? That’s the normal one-command way to do this, and it works fine for brand-new repos in most setups — but on this machine it refused with “the remote origin does not have a branch named gh-pages”, even freshly initialized, even with --no-prompt/piped confirmation. The worktree approach above is what actually worked and is what’s used now. If a future Quarto/environment update fixes this, quarto publish gh-pages is the simpler path to retry.
Gotcha hit while setting this up: don’t run the orphan-branch steps (git checkout --orphan, git rm -rf .) directly inside the r-ready working copy, even “temporarily” — if a cd into a worktree silently fails (e.g. Windows’ ~260-character path limit, easy to hit with a deeply nested temp folder + this extension’s long filenames), those commands run in r-ready itself instead and wipe the working directory. Always use a separate, short-path worktree (e.g. C:\ghpwt-tmp, not something nested under a long temp/session path), and verify pwd before running anything destructive. (Recovery, if it happens again: the files are still safe in the main branch’s history — git switch main restores everything.)
Live URL: https://tahereh-gh.github.io/basic-r-course/ — GitHub enabled Pages automatically the moment the gh-pages branch was pushed; no manual Settings step was needed.
See https://quarto.org/docs/publishing/github-pages.html for details.



r-ready/
├── _quarto.yml          site config, navigation
├── styles.scss           theme + small custom styles
├── index.qmd             home page
├── missions/              the "Before the course" missions, 00–06
├── help/                  the "Help! 😱" troubleshooting section
├── downloads/             files students download (participants.csv)
├── _includes/             shared JS (quiz + R Passport interactivity)
└── _extensions/           quarto-webr, for Mission 3's live R cells

title: ❓ Object not found
text: Error in mean(age) : object 'age' not found

title: ❓ Object not found
text: Error in mean(age) : object 'age' not found

title: ❓ Object not found
text:
What it means
Remember the Mission 3 model: an object is a labelled box. This error means the box you’re asking for was never actually created — R looked for something named age and came up empty.
That happens for one of a few very ordinary reasons, almost never because R is “broken”:

The line that creates it never ran. You wrote age <- 25 but ran later lines without ever running that one — easy to do when jumping around a script instead of running top to bottom.
It’s a typo. age and Age are different boxes to R. So are age and age (a trailing space, if it snuck into a copy-paste).
You restarted R. Every object you’ve created lives only in the current R session. Restarting R (or reopening RStudio) empties all the boxes — your script still has the code to recreate them, but you have to actually run it again.
An earlier line silently failed. If the line meant to create age threw its own error, R never got to create the box, and everything after it that depends on age will fail too.

title: ❓ Object not found
text:
The fix

Check the Environment pane (top-right in RStudio) — it lists every object that currently exists. If age isn’t there, it’s genuinely not been created yet in this session.
Run your script from the top, in order (Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + Enter runs the whole thing, or Ctrl/Cmd + Alt + B runs from the beginning to your cursor). This fixes the “ran things out of order” case immediately.
Scroll up to the line that’s supposed to create the object and check it ran without its own error first.
Check spelling and case against exactly how you wrote it originally.

Still stuck? Run the specific line that’s supposed to create the object, on its own, and see what it actually does — that isolates the problem immediately.

title: 🔍 R cannot find my file
text:
Error: 'data/participants.csv' does not exist in current working directory
or
Warning message:
cannot open file 'data/participants.csv': No such file or directory

title: 🔍 R cannot find my file
text:
Error: 'data/participants.csv' does not exist in current working directory
or
Warning message:
cannot open file 'data/participants.csv': No such file or directory

title: 🔍 R cannot find my file
text:
What it means
R searched for that file starting from its current 🏠 (see Mission 2) and didn’t find it there. This is almost never a “your file is missing” problem — it’s a “R is looking in the wrong place, or the name doesn’t match exactly” problem.

title: 🔍 R cannot find my file
text:
The fix
Work through these in order — one of them is almost always it:

Run getwd(). Does the folder it reports match your project? If not, you likely opened a script directly instead of the .Rproj file — close RStudio and reopen via the .Rproj.
Run list.files("data") (or whichever folder should hold the file). Is your file actually listed? Check the spelling exactly — participant.csv isn’t participants.csv. Capitalisation (Data vs data) usually doesn’t matter on Windows or Mac, but it’s still worth matching exactly, since it will matter the moment this script runs on Linux or a shared server.
Check the file extension isn’t hidden. Windows sometimes hides extensions, so a file that looks like participants.csv in File Explorer might actually be participants.csv.xlsx or similar. In File Explorer, turn on “File name extensions” (View tab) to check.
Check your path uses forward slashes (data/participants.csv), not backslashes.

Still stuck? Take a screenshot of the exact error and the output of getwd() and list.files(".") — that combination is almost always enough to spot it immediately.

title: 🧩 My code just doesn’t run
text:
> is R saying “ready for a new command.” + means “I’m still waiting — you haven’t finished your sentence yet.” Usually an unclosed (, [, {, or a quote mark that’s missing its partner.



Press Esc in the Console to cancel and get back to >. Then look at what you ran for a missing closing bracket or quote — count them if you have to. This is exactly what happened in Mission 4’s mean(age example.

title: 🧩 My code just doesn’t run
text:
> is R saying “ready for a new command.” + means “I’m still waiting — you haven’t finished your sentence yet.” Usually an unclosed (, [, {, or a quote mark that’s missing its partner.



Press Esc in the Console to cancel and get back to >. Then look at what you ran for a missing closing bracket or quote — count them if you have to. This is exactly what happened in Mission 4’s mean(age example.

title: 🧩 My code just doesn’t run
section: Symptom: you ran a line and nothing seems to have happened
text:
Symptom: you ran a line and nothing seems to have happened

What it means
Probably not true — R almost always does something, even if it’s invisible. Check:

Did you actually run it? Clicking into a line doesn’t run it. In RStudio, Ctrl/Cmd + Enter runs the current line (or current selection) and moves on.
Was something else highlighted/selected when you pressed run, so a different chunk of code executed instead of what you meant?
Did it run but assign silently? age <- 25 deliberately produces no visible output — that’s normal. Type age on its own afterward to confirm it worked.

title: 🧩 My code just doesn’t run
section: Symptom: red text vs. yellow/orange text
text:
Symptom: red text vs. yellow/orange text

What it means
These are not the same thing, and it matters which one you have:

Error (usually shown in red) — R stopped. Whatever you were trying to do did not happen. Everything below this that depends on it will also fail.
Warning (usually yellow/orange) — R finished anyway, but wants you to know something looked off (e.g. NAs introduced by coercion). Worth reading, not automatically a problem — but also not automatically fine. Check whether the result looks like what you expected.

Still stuck? Copy the exact text from the Console — the difference between “nothing ran” and “something ran but silently” is usually obvious once someone else can see exactly what’s there.

title: Help! 😱
text:
Stuck? Start here — before or during the course. This page exists so that in class, the answer can be “have a look at Help → [topic]” instead of re-explaining the same beginner snag five times a day.
Pick what’s happening:

🔍 R cannot find my file — Error: 'data/x.csv' does not exist and friends.
📦 A package won’t install — install.packages() fails, or library() says it’s not there.
❓ Object not found — Error: object 'x' not found.
🧩 My code just doesn’t run — nothing happens, or the console shows a + and won’t stop.

Not seeing your problem? That’s expected — this page grows as real questions come up. If you’re a student hitting this during the live course, just ask; if you’re Tahereh or Genona adding to this page later, the pattern for each entry is: what you see → what it means → the fix, kept to a few lines each.

title: 📦 A package won’t install
text: This is actually two different problems that look similar. Work out which one you have first.

title: 📦 A package won’t install
text:
Problem A: install.packages(...) itself fails

What you see
Warning message:
package 'tidyverse' is not available for this version of R
or the install just hangs, or errors partway through with something mentioning a “CRAN mirror” or a network timeout.


What it means
R couldn’t download or install the package — usually a connectivity issue, not something wrong with your code.


The fix

Check you’re actually connected to the internet (obvious, but it’s the most common cause).
Try a different CRAN mirror: install.packages("tidyverse", repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org") sidesteps a slow or unreachable default mirror.
Restart R (Session → Restart R in RStudio) and try again — a half-finished previous install can block a new one.
Check the package name is spelled correctly. install.packages("tidyvers") fails for a completely different reason than a network issue, and the message can look similar at a glance.

title: 📦 A package won’t install
section: Problem B: it installed, but library(...) won’t load it
text:
Problem B: it installed, but library(...) won’t load it

What you see
Error in library(tidyvers) : there is no package called 'tidyvers'


What it means
Either it’s a typo (R is case-sensitive here too — Tidyverse ≠ tidyverse), or it really did install, but into a different R library location than the one this R session is using (common if you have more than one version of R installed).


The fix

Run installed.packages()[, "Package"] and search the output for the name you expect — if it’s not there, it isn’t actually installed; go back to Problem A.
Double check the exact spelling and lowercase/uppercase against the CRAN package page or the course materials.
If it’s listed but still won’t load, restart R and try library() again before anything else runs.

Still stuck? Copy the exact red text and ask — package installation problems are usually solved in under a minute once someone can see the actual message.

title: R Ready
text:
Before the course starts, complete a few short missions.
You don’t need to know R yet. The goal isn’t to learn R early — it’s to make sure your computer, and you, are ready to hit the ground running on day one. Everything here is done at your own pace, in your own RStudio.

text:
Your missions

Stuck on something later, even during the course itself? Check Help! 😱 — it’s the same page your instructors will point you to in class instead of re-explaining the same thing five times.






TipWhy bother with this before day one?



The most common thing that slows people down on day one isn’t R itself — it’s things like “where did I save that file” or “why can’t R find my data.” Those aren’t R problems, they’re computer-setup problems, and they’re much less stressful to sort out now, alone, than in a room full of people on a tight schedule.


Ready? Start with Mission 0 →

title: 🏠 Mission 1: Give your analysis a home
text: ⏱️ About 10 minutes · do this in RStudio
crumbs: 🏠 Mission 1: Give your analysis a home

title: 🏠 Mission 1: Give your analysis a home
text:
The idea
Every analysis needs a home base — one folder that contains everything it needs: the data, the code, the output. In RStudio, that home base is called a Project.

📁 Project folder = the home of your analysis 📁 data/ = where your data lives 📁 R/ = where your scripts live 📁 figures/ = where output can go

Without a project, R doesn’t know where “home” is, and you end up typing full file paths like C:/Users/Anna/Desktop/finally/actual-project-v2-FINAL/ — which breaks the moment you rename a folder, move the project, or open it on a different computer. A project fixes that: everything is found relative to the project, so the folder can move, get renamed, or get zipped and sent to a collaborator, and it still works.






TipWhy not just use folders on your Desktop?



You can — RStudio doesn’t force you to use Projects. But without one, R’s “starting point” (see Mission 2) is whatever folder happened to be active when RStudio launched, which changes unpredictably. A Project pins that starting point to one fixed place.
crumbs: 🏠 Mission 1: Give your analysis a home

title: 🏠 Mission 1: Give your analysis a home
text:
Your task
Create this exact structure:
my-first-r-project/
│
├── my-first-r-project.Rproj
│
├── data/
│   └── participants.csv
│
├── R/
│   └── analysis.R
│
└── figures/
Step by step:

Open RStudio.
Go to File → New Project… → New Directory → New Project.
Name it my-first-r-project and choose where to save it (Desktop or Documents is fine).
Click Create Project. RStudio will reopen inside your new project — check the top-right corner, it should now show my-first-r-project.
In the Files pane (bottom-right), click New Folder and create two folders: data and figures.
Create a folder called R, and inside it, a new R script: File → New File → R Script, save it as R/analysis.R.
⬇ Download participants.csv and save it into your data/ folder. (A file you find yourself might not open cleanly — this one’s guaranteed to work, and you’ll use it again in later missions.)







ImportantThe one habit that prevents 90% of “R can’t find my stuff” problems



Always open your project by double-clicking the .Rproj file — never by opening a loose .R script directly. Opening the .Rproj file is what tells R “start here.” Opening a script by itself doesn’t.
crumbs: 🏠 Mission 1: Give your analysis a home

title: 🏠 Mission 1: Give your analysis a home
section: Where do I actually type code?
text:
Where do I actually type code?
RStudio’s window is split into panes. You only need to know two of them for now:






①
②
③
④

(This is a real screenshot from this project’s own RStudio — R 4.4.1, Project: (None) in the top-right, which is exactly the “before you make a Project” state this mission fixes.)

① Source — a text editor for your .R script. Nothing here runs on its own; it’s just saved text until you tell R to run it.
② Console — where code is actually executed, one command at a time. Anything you type directly here runs the instant you press Enter.
The connection between them: put your cursor on a line in the Source pane and press Ctrl+Enter (Windows) or ⌘+Enter (Mac) — or click the Run button — and that line gets sent down to the Console and runs.







NoteWhat are Environment and Files/Plots/Help for?





Not essential today, but for context: ③ Environment lists every object R currently has in memory (you’ll create your first ones in Mission 3). ④ Files/Plots/Help is a set of tabs — browse folders, view any plots you make, or read a function’s documentation.




Try both
In R/analysis.R:

Type 2 + 2 and press Ctrl+Enter (or ⌘+Enter) with your cursor on that line. Watch it appear in the Console below, with the answer.
Now click directly in the Console itself, type 2 + 2 again, and press Enter.

Same result, two different starting points. The difference that matters: only what you write in the script gets saved when you save the file — anything typed straight into the Console is gone the moment you close RStudio. That’s why real work goes in the script, and the Console is more for quick one-off checks.
crumbs: 🏠 Mission 1: Give your analysis a home

title: 🏠 Mission 1: Give your analysis a home
text:
Check yourself

Your project has a .Rproj file at the top level.
You have data/, R/, and figures/ folders inside it.
The top-right corner of RStudio shows your project’s name — not “Project: (None)”.

If all three are true, you’re done. If RStudio says “Project: (None)”, you opened a file instead of the project — close RStudio, find my-first-r-project.Rproj in your file explorer, and double-click that.
Next up: Mission 2 — Help R find your files →

title: 🗣️ Mission 3: Learn R’s language
text: ⏱️ About 10 minutes · try it live right here, no install needed

title: 🗣️ Mission 3: Learn R’s language
section: R isn’t a list of commands — it’s a small language
text:
R isn’t a list of commands — it’s a small language
You don’t need to memorize R. You need to recognize three pieces of grammar, because once you can read them, most R code becomes a sentence instead of a puzzle.
Every example below is live — click into the code and press Run, or just edit it and run your own version. Nothing you do here can break anything.

title: 🗣️ Mission 3: Learn R’s language
text:
1. Objects: labelled boxes
age <- 25
Read <- as “store this, under this name.” This line means: take the number 25, put it in a box, label the box age. From now on, typing age anywhere gets you back what’s in the box.

🌐 Try it live — run it, then change 25 to your own age and run it again


Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.






NoteWhy the arrow, not =?



age = 25 also works in R, but <- is the convention, and it’s worth keeping: it visually points in the direction the value is flowing — into the box.

title: 🗣️ Mission 3: Learn R’s language
text:
2. Functions: verbs that need ingredients
mean(age)
A function name followed by parentheses is a verb — and whatever’s inside the parentheses are its ingredients (arguments). Read mean(age) as “compute the mean, using age as the ingredient.” Some verbs need more than one ingredient, separated by commas — round(3.14159, 2) reads as “round 3.14159, to 2 decimal places.”

🌐 Try it live


Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

title: 🗣️ Mission 3: Learn R’s language
text:
3. Vectors: R’s basic unit
R rarely stores just one thing — it stores vectors, which are just ordered collections of values of the same type. Here’s the twist: a single number, like the age above, actually is a vector — one with a length of 1. That’s why functions like mean() work the same way whether you give them one number or a thousand.

🌐 Try it live


Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

title: 🗣️ Mission 3: Learn R’s language
section: Try it: translate before you run
text:
Try it: translate before you run
Before you run this one, write in plain English (out loud, or in your head) what each line does. Then run it and check yourself against the last two lines.

title: 🔬 Mission 5: Your first research dataset
text:
⏱️ About 10 minutes · do this in RStudio, using your Mission 1 project
Time to put Missions 1–3 to work on something real.

title: 🔬 Mission 5: Your first research dataset
text:
Get the data
Good news — you already have it. Remember participants.csv, the file you downloaded into data/ back in Mission 1? That’s what you’ll use here.
(Skipped that step, or can’t find it? ⬇ Download participants.csv and save it into your project’s data/ folder now.)

title: 🔬 Mission 5: Your first research dataset
text:
Import it
In R/analysis.R:
participants <- read.csv("data/participants.csv")
Notice the shape of that path — "data/participants.csv" — it’s the Mission 2 mental model again: start at 🏠, open data, find participants.csv.






NoteNotice what you didn’t need



No install.packages(), no library() — reading a .csv is something base R can already do, no extra tools required. Later in the course you’ll meet library(), which loads add-on packages: extra tools that give R abilities it doesn’t have out of the box. Don’t worry about what that means yet — we’ll cover it properly on the course itself. For now, just notice that plenty of real work doesn’t need it.

title: 🔬 Mission 5: Your first research dataset
text:
Get to know it
Don’t analyze it yet — just look around, the way you’d skim a paper before reading it closely.
participants             # print it
str(participants)         # what's the structure? how many variables, what types?
dim(participants)          # rows, columns
names(participants)        # just the column names
summary(participants)      # a quick five-number summary of each column

title: 🔬 Mission 5: Your first research dataset
section: Answer this from the output alone
text:
Answer this from the output alone
Using what dim() or str() told you: how many participants are in this dataset, and what does each row represent? (Hint: look at the column names — id, age, group, score. One row is one what?)
You don’t need to write the answer anywhere. If you can say it out loud in a sentence, you’ve done the mission.
